briefing:
Day 27: Kaliningrad Phase 1 at 54% (730/1,350) after just two days — Russia exceeding targets. Latvia ratifies 78-12, Estonia ratifies 89-6 — all three Baltic states now formally bound. First ESAF verification visit at Asipovichy confirms IAEA certification holds. Magyar survives first confidence vote 112-87.

The implementation pace is remarkable. Russia's decision to front-load Kaliningrad departures suggests Moscow wants early compliance credit, possibly to accelerate the sanctions relief timeline. The OSCE reports zero discrepancies between declared and observed personnel movements.

ESAF Asipovichy inspection: 8 hours, unrestricted access, all seals intact, radiation signatures confirmed. Belarusian transitional council broadcast inspection live — maximum transparency.

Markets: Oil $71, ruble 109/USD. European gas futures down another 2%. Hungarian forint strengthening on EU fund unfreezing news. Implementation Day 2 of 90.
narrative:
Day 27 brings a cascade of ratifications that transforms the Istanbul Framework from a signed document into binding international law across the Baltic region. At 10:00, the Latvian Saeima votes 78-12 to ratify. At 14:30, the Estonian Riigikogu follows with 89-6 — the largest margin in Estonian parliamentary history for a security agreement. By evening, all three Baltic states have formally ratified, and the Framework's collective security provisions are legally operational across the most vulnerable stretch of NATO's eastern flank.

In Kaliningrad, the drawdown accelerates. Day 2 sees 418 additional personnel depart — the 7th Motor Rifle Regiment's support elements, traveling by rail through Lithuania under OSCE escort to the Russian mainland. The OSCE reports that Russia has exceeded its Day 2 target by 6%, a signal that Moscow wants to build compliance momentum ahead of the Day 30 warhead planning milestone. The total now stands at 730 of 1,350 — Phase 1 is 54% complete in just two days.

The first ESAF verification visit takes place at the former Asipovichy nuclear storage site in Belarus. A team of 12 inspectors — led by IAEA Deputy Director Massimo Aparo and accompanied by European Three verification officers — conducts an 8-hour site inspection. Their preliminary finding confirms the IAEA Category A certification: all monitoring seals are intact, radiation signatures match declared inventory, and the Belarusian transitional council has provided unrestricted access. The inspection is broadcast live on Belarusian state television — a deliberately transparent contrast to the Lukashenko era.

In Budapest, the Magyar government's first week produces tangible results. The European Commission announces it will begin processing Hungary's EUR 22B fund unfreezing request on an expedited timeline, with the first tranche of EUR 5.5B potentially available within 60 days. Magyar's approval rating rises to 35% — still fragile, but on a clear upward trajectory. His coalition, assembled from reformed Fidesz moderates, TISZA, and opposition parties, survives its first parliamentary confidence vote 112-87.

surprises: During the Asipovichy inspection, IAEA Deputy Director Aparo discovers something unexpected: a handwritten note taped to the inside of a monitoring seal cabinet, left by a Belarusian military technician during the crisis. It reads, in Russian: 'To whoever opens this next — we kept them safe. We did our duty. Please remember that ordinary soldiers prevented catastrophe.' Aparo photographs the note with the technician's permission. When it surfaces on social media that evening, it goes viral — a reminder that behind the grand diplomacy of Istanbul, individual acts of conscience by Belarusian military personnel who defied Lukashenko were what prevented the warheads from being moved during the most dangerous hours of the crisis.
